text: Batting is the discipline in cricket concerned with scoring runs and protecting the wicket. A batter faces deliveries bowled from twenty-two yards (20.12 metres) away and must make a continuous series of decisions - whether to play or leave, whether to come forward or go back, whether to defend or attack, and whether to run. This document is the batting-focused member of a ten-document cricket corpus. Its primary subject is batting technique and batting strategy. It intentionally overlaps with other documents in the corpus on the topics of international formats (covered primarily in Document 06), powerplays and field restrictions (Documents 05, 07, 08), playing spin (Document 03), facing fast bowling (Document 02) and famous innings (Document 10). Where a topic overlaps, this document treats it from the batter's point of view. Key definitional note used throughout: a dismissal ends a batter's innings; a not out batter remains at the crease when the innings closes. Ten dismissals end a team innings in the standard eleven-player format, because a single remaining batter cannot bat alone.

Technique in batting is not decoration. It exists to solve three recurring problems:
1. Time - a delivery at 145 km/h reaches the batter in roughly 0.4 seconds.
2. Alignment - the bat must meet the ball with the face square to the intended direction.
3. Repeatability - the same movement must work on the first ball and the threehundredth.
A technique that produces runs but collapses under pressure is incomplete. Coaches therefore judge technique by its error tolerance : how far the ball can deviate from the expected line and length before the method fails.

The stance is the position adopted before the bowler releases the ball.
- Feet : roughly shoulder-width apart, parallel to or slightly across the crease, with weight distributed evenly or marginally on the balls of the feet.
- Knees : slightly flexed, never locked. Locked knees delay the first movement.
- Head : both eyes level and facing the bowler. Level eyes are the single most repeated coaching cue in batting, because a tilted head distorts the perceived line of the ball.
- Hands : resting near the top of the back pad, with the bat either grounded behind the back foot or held up in a pre-cocked position.
Open vs closed stance. A side-on (closed) stance presents the shoulder to the bowler and favours driving through the off side. An open stance rotates the front shoulder towards the leg side, improving access to the leg side and helping batters who struggle to pick up the ball from a wide-of-the-crease angle. Neither is universally correct; the open stance has become more common in T20 cricket because it assists the pull and the leg-side slog.

The grip governs the range of shots available.

A grip fault to watch for is splitting the hands - leaving a gap between top and bottom hand. It reduces control of the bat face and is a frequent cause of leading-edge dismissals.

The backlift is the upward movement of the bat before the downswing. Two broad families exist:
- Straight backlift - the bat rises over the stumps or over middle stump. It shortens the path back to the ball and suits a batter who plays straight.
- Looped or angled backlift - the bat rises towards second slip or gully before looping back into line. It generates more bat speed and is common among powerful drivers of the ball.
The critical measure is not direction but timing of the down-swing : the bat should begin coming down as the front foot lands, not before and not after.

Footwork positions the head, and the head positions everything else.
- Front-foot movement : the front foot moves towards the pitch of the ball, ideally landing with the toe pointing down the wicket rather than towards square leg.
- Back-foot movement : the back foot moves back and across towards off stump, creating depth in the crease and time to play the ball late.
- Trigger movements : small preparatory movements made as the bowler enters delivery stride, such as a small back-and-across step or a press forward. Trigger movements must be complete before release; a batter still moving at release is effectively playing blind.
A common measurable fault is the planted front foot - the front leg moves forward but the weight remains back, leaving the batter neither forward nor back. This is the classic precursor to an LBW dismissal (see Document 07 for the full LBW law).

Used against a ball of good length pitched on or just outside off stump. The front foot moves to the pitch of the ball, the head is over the ball, the bat comes down straight with soft hands, and the ball is deadened at the feet. The bat face should be angled slightly downward to keep the ball on the ground.

Used against short-of-a-length deliveries. The back foot goes back and across, the batter rises slightly, and the ball is played down under the eyes. Soft hands are again essential - hard hands lead to catches to gully, slip and short leg.

Leaving the ball is a scoring-free but valuable act. A disciplined leave outside off stump forces the bowler to bowl straighter, which opens leg-side scoring options. In Test cricket a top-order batter may leave 25-35% of deliveries in the first hour with a new ball. Leaving technique : the bat is raised above the shoulder and the hands are lifted away from the body line, so an unexpected bounce cannot deflect the ball onto the stumps or to slip.

The cover drive is often described as the most attractive and most dangerous shot in cricket: it is played away from the body, and a small misjudgement of swing or seam movement produces an edge to the slip cordon.

- Pull : played to a short ball from around chest height, swinging the bat horizontally to the leg side, rolling the wrists to keep it down. The back foot pivots.
- Hook : played to a ball at or above shoulder height, usually with the intention of clearing fine leg or square leg. It carries higher risk because the ball is played close to the eyes.
Field placements directly target these shots: a deep square leg and a deep fine leg are the standard responses to a batter who pulls well (see Document 05 for field-placement detail).

- Square cut : short and wide outside off, played square of the wicket with a horizontal bat, weight on the back foot.
- Late cut : played with a delayed, angled face to steer the ball behind point, particularly effective against spin.
- Upper cut : played to a short, wide, rising delivery over the slip cordon or third-man region. It is essentially a controlled edge and is a high-risk, high-reward limited-overs option.

The sweep family is primarily an answer to spin bowling and is treated from the bowler's perspective in Document 03.
- Conventional sweep : front knee to the ground, horizontal bat, ball hit square or fine on the leg side.
- Paddle sweep / lap : a deflection rather than a hit, sending the ball fine of square leg.
- Slog sweep : a lofted sweep aimed over deep midwicket, played from a wider base and with a higher backlift.
- Reverse sweep : the hands reverse on the handle (or the wrists rotate) and the ball is swept to the off side behind point. Its tactical value is that it defeats a packed leg-side field.
- Switch hit : the batter reverses both grip and stance before release, effectively converting a right-hander into a left-hander. It is legal under current playing conditions; the bowler is not permitted to change his announced arm or side without informing the umpire, which is why the shot is tactically asymmetric.

Lofted hitting depends on three variables: bat speed , contact position relative to the body , and launch angle . Coaches teach a lofted drive with the head still and the ball struck under the eyes; the elevation comes from the bat's downward-then-upward arc, not from leaning back.

A settled bowler bowling to a settled batter with a set field is a stable system. Rotating strike breaks it: it forces field adjustments, changes the bowler's line, and prevents the 'dot-ball pressure' that precedes most collapses.

Three calls are used: yes , no , and wait . The conventional rule is that the batter with the better view calls: the striker calls for balls hit in front of square, and the non-striker calls for balls hit behind square.

- Run the first run hard, in case a second is available.
- Carry the bat in the hand nearer the fielder's throwing side so the body is turned correctly.
- Slide the bat along the ground through the crease rather than stabbing at the line - a bat bouncing up as it crosses the line is a recurring source of run-out dismissals.
- Turn by dropping low and pushing off the outside foot.

Strike management is the deliberate allocation of strike. Examples:
- A set batter takes a single off the fifth ball to retain strike for the next over.
- A tail-ender is 'farmed' - protected by the recognised batter taking singles late in the over.
- Against a dangerous bowler, the stronger player of that bowling type deliberately takes the majority of the strike (a match-up decision, treated tactically in Document 08).

Facing fast bowling requires a shorter, simpler method. The elements:
- Watch the ball out of the hand. Pick up the release point rather than the run-up.
- Play late. Allowing the ball to travel further reduces the effect of late swing or seam movement.
- Play beneath the eyes. Contact in front of the pad, under the head.
- Judge length early, line late. Length determines forward or back; line determines the shot.
Swing. Conventional swing moves in the air toward or away from the batter; the response is to play later and to trust the leave outside off. Reverse swing , which typically appears with an older ball, moves in the opposite direction to what the shiny side suggests and is most dangerous as a full delivery or a yorker. Document 02 covers the bowling mechanics of both. Short-pitched bowling. Three legitimate responses exist: evade (duck or sway), defend (backfoot defence with soft hands), or attack (pull or hook). A batter should decide the default response before the spell, not during the delivery.
Playing spin well is a function of decisiveness : the two safe positions are fully forward to the pitch of the ball and fully back in the crease. The dangerous position is the half-forward press.

1. Use the feet - advance down the pitch to convert a good length into a half-volley.
2. Depth in the crease - go back to convert a good length into a short ball, giving time to cut or pull.
3. Sweep - remove turn and bounce from the equation by playing across the line with the pitch.
4. Work the ball into gaps - soft-handed pushes into the off side and leg side for singles.
Against the leg-spinner , the ball leaving a right-hander is the most dangerous delivery; the googly turning back in is the wicket-taking variation. Against the off-spinner , the ball spinning in threatens LBW and bowled, while the arm ball that holds its line threatens the outside edge. Document 03 describes these deliveries from the bowler's perspective.

The central currency is balls faced , not runs scored. A top-order Test batter's first thirty deliveries are the highest-risk period of the innings, because the bat has not yet calibrated to the pace and bounce of the surface. Strategy in a Test innings: survive the new ball, accumulate against the older ball, accelerate before a declaration.

- Powerplay 1 (overs 1-10) : only two fielders permitted outside the 30-yard circle. Batting intent is to exploit the gaps without losing early wickets.
- Middle overs (11-40) : a maximum of four fielders outside the circle. Strike rotation dominates; the objective is typically to reach the 40-over mark with wickets in hand.
- Death overs (41-50) : a maximum of five fielders outside the circle. Boundary hitting and yorker counter-measures dominate.

- Powerplay (overs 1-6) : two fielders outside the circle. A frequent modern approach is to maximise boundary attempts in this phase while accepting a higher dismissal risk.
- Middle overs (7-15) : five fielders outside the circle; spinners often bowl here, and the batting aim is to avoid consecutive dot balls.
- Death overs (16-20) : boundary-hitting phase against yorkers, wide slower balls and short balls.
The precise powerplay regulations are set out in Document 07; the bowling response to each phase appears in Documents 02 and 03; the tactical framing appears in Document 08.
A partnership is a joint innings by two batters and is more than the sum of the two contributions, because the pair share the strike, share information about the conditions, and share pressure.

- Anchor - occupies the crease, protects against collapse, bats deep into the innings.
- Aggressor - takes on the bowling and raises the run rate.
- Finisher - enters late in a limited-overs innings with an explicit brief to hit boundaries.
Partnership building follows a loose sequence: survive the first twenty balls together, agree on the target bowler, agree on the target phase for acceleration, and re-set after each wicket or drinks break.

Scenario A - Test, second morning, overcast, new ball. The ball is swinging. The correct batting response is a narrowed shot range: forward defence, leave, and leg-side clip only. Driving is deferred until the ball stops moving. Scoring rate is expected to be low; the measure of success is balls survived rather than runs. Scenario B - ODI chase, 62 required from 60 balls, 5 wickets in hand. The required run rate is 6.20. The batting pair should identify the weakest of the remaining bowling options, target two overs of that bowler for boundaries, and otherwise take singles. Panic here almost always takes the form of attacking the best bowler. Scenario C - T20, 24 required from the final over. The batting side needs roughly one boundary every other ball. The strategy is to pre-select a hitting zone, stand deep in the crease to turn yorkers into low full tosses, and take any available two on a mishit. Scenario D - Test, final session, defending for a draw. Runs are irrelevant. The batters
should maximise deliveries faced per over by refusing singles late in the over when the tail is at the other end, and should treat every delivery as a leave-or-defend decision.

Batting rests on a small number of repeatable physical actions - stance, grip, backlift, footwork - and a much larger number of decisions. Technique determines what is possible; decision-making determines what is chosen. The formats differ less in the shots available than in the acceptable level of risk per delivery: a Test batter optimises for survival, an ODI batter for a controlled acceleration curve, and a T20 batter for boundary frequency. Cross-references within this corpus: Document 02 (fast bowling mechanics, yorkers, reverse swing), Document 03 (spin variations and field settings), Document 05 (field placements that constrain shot selection), Document 06 (formats and international structure), Document 07 (LBW, no-balls, powerplay law), Document 08 (batting order and match-ups), Document 09 (strike rate, batting average and their limitations) and Document 10 (famous innings).

Fast bowling is the discipline of delivering the cricket ball at high velocity, using pace, bounce, swing and seam movement to dismiss batters or restrict scoring. This document is the pacebowling member of a ten-document cricket corpus. Its primary subject is fast-bowling technique and tactics. It deliberately overlaps with Document 01 (batting against pace), Document 03 (spin bowling, for contrast), Document 04 (wicketkeeping standing back), Document 05 (field placements), Document 06 (international formats and famous bowlers), Document 07 (no-ball and wide law) and Document 08 (bowling changes and match-ups).

Pace is produced by a chain of movements, each contributing energy that is transferred up through the body and released through the bowling arm. A break anywhere in that chain leaks speed. The chain, in order: run-up → gather (load) → back-foot contact → front-foot contact (brace) → hip and shoulder rotation → arm acceleration → release → follow-through.
Three physical qualities matter most: front-leg bracing strength , hip-shoulder separation (the angular difference between the hip line and shoulder line at back-foot contact), and trunk flexion through release. Studies of bowling biomechanics consistently identify a straighter, more strongly braced front leg with faster release speeds, because a collapsing front knee absorbs energy that would otherwise transfer to the ball.

The run-up exists to deliver the body to the crease with controllable momentum and in a repeatable rhythm.
- Length : typically 15-25 metres for a fast bowler; shorter for fast-medium.
- Acceleration profile : gradual build, with the fastest strides in the final third. A run-up that peaks too early leaves the bowler decelerating into the crease.
- Repeatability : the run-up must be measured and marked so the bowler arrives at the same point with the same stride pattern. An inconsistent run-up is the most common root cause of no-balls.
- The gather (load) : the penultimate movement in which the bowler jumps, turns the body and raises the non-bowling arm. This is where the bowler converts horizontal momentum into a coiled rotational position.

Front-on, Shoulder/hip alignment at back-foot contact = Shoulders and hips facing the batter. Front-on, Characteristics = Associated with inswing and seam-up bowling. The mixed action is discouraged in coaching not because it fails to produce pace but because the counter-rotation it requires is linked to lower-back stress fractures, especially in adolescent bowlers.

At front-foot contact the bowler's foot must land with some part of it behind the popping crease for the delivery to be legal. Overstepping is a no-ball (Document 07). At international level a no-ball in a limited-overs innings also concedes a free hit , meaning the batter cannot be dismissed off the next legal delivery except by run out, hit the ball twice or obstructing the field.

Release height and release point determine the angle of attack. A taller bowler releasing from a higher point generates steeper bounce from the same length. Bowling close to the stumps creates a straighter line and brings LBW and bowled into play; bowling wide of the crease creates an angle across the batter and is used to attack the outside edge or to cramp a batter for room.

The seam is the raised stitched ridge around the ball. Holding the ball with the seam upright and delivering it with the seam spinning backwards on a stable axis is the foundation of both swing and seam movement. A scrambled seam - deliberately releasing with the seam wobbling - removes predictable movement and is used as a variation, particularly on surfaces with pronounced grass.

Conventional swing occurs when one side of the ball is kept smooth and shiny while the other roughens. The ball is held with the seam angled toward the intended direction of swing.
- Outswing (to a right-handed batter): seam angled towards slip, shiny side on the leg side. The ball moves away from the batter. The classic dismissal is caught behind or in the slip cordon.
- Inswing : seam angled towards fine leg, shiny side on the off side. The ball moves in towards the batter. The classic dismissals are bowled and LBW.
Swing is most pronounced early in the innings with a new, hard ball, and is commonly associated with humid or overcast conditions, though the physics of the relationship remains debated.

Reverse swing appears with an older ball, typically after 30-40 overs, when one side has become significantly rougher than the other and the ball is bowled at high speed. Counterintuitively, the ball swings towards the shiny side rather than away from it. It is most dangerous as a full delivery or a yorker, because the movement occurs late and the batter has committed to a shot. Only legal means of ball maintenance - polishing on clothing, drying, and cleaning - are permitted; artificially altering the condition of the ball is an offence under the Laws.

Seam movement occurs off the pitch rather than in the air: the ball lands on the seam and deviates. It is largely a function of the surface and is less controllable than swing, which is why bowlers who 'hit the seam' aim for a consistent good length and allow the pitch to do the work.

- The good-length seam-up ball. The stock delivery. It succeeds because it forces the batter to decide between front and back foot.
- The yorker. Aimed at the base of the stumps or the batter's toes. It is the primary death-over weapon because it is extremely difficult to hit for a boundary, but a missed yorker becomes a half-volley or full toss.
- The bouncer. A short ball aimed at the batter's head or chest. Under current playing conditions, a limited number of deliveries above shoulder height are permitted per over; exceeding it results in a no-ball call. The bouncer works both as a wicket-taking delivery (top edges to fine leg) and as a set-up delivery that pushes the batter onto the back foot before a full ball.

- The slower ball. Released with reduced pace to disrupt timing. Variants include the off-cutter (fingers pulled down the off side of the ball), the leg-cutter (fingers pulled across the leg side), the back-of-the-hand slower ball , the split-finger slower ball and the knuckle ball . The essential requirement is that the arm speed remains unchanged, so that only the ball is slow, not the action.
- The wide yorker. Bowled full and outside the batter's reach in the death overs, usually protected by a deep point and deep third.
- The wobble-seam ball. A scrambled-seam delivery that may move either way off the pitch, denying the batter a predictable direction.

In Test cricket the fielding side may take a new ball after a set number of overs (80 in the standard playing conditions), which typically triggers a return to full, attacking lengths.

During the first powerplay only two fielders are permitted outside the thirty-yard circle, so the bowler has almost no protection square of the wicket. The consequences for pace bowling are direct:
- Bowl fuller than usual to bring the stumps and the edge into play, accepting the risk of the drive.
- Use the slip cordon while it is justified; a wicket in the powerplay is worth more than two runs saved.
- Avoid the short ball early unless the surface offers steep bounce, because the pull has an unprotected boundary.

With four fielders permitted outside the circle in an ODI (five in a T20 after the powerplay), the pace bowler's objective shifts to dot-ball creation and wicket-taking through change of pace. Back-of-a-length bowling into the pitch with a protected square boundary is the standard method.

Death bowling is the highest-skill phase in limited-overs pace bowling. Core principles:
1. Have two plans per batter, not one. A batter who has picked the yorker will hit it.
2. Execute to the wider margin. A missed yorker aimed at middle stump is a hittable full toss; a missed wide yorker is often merely a wide.
3. Use the field. Wide yorkers require a deep point and deep third; bouncers require deep square and deep fine leg.
4. Vary the crease position. Changing between close to the stumps and wide of the crease alters the angle without changing the ball.

Field settings follow the plan, not the reverse. Typical configurations (overlapping with Document 05):
- Attacking new-ball field : three slips, gully, point, cover, mid-off, mid-on, fine leg, square leg.
- Containing middle-overs field (ODI) : slip or none, point, cover, mid-off, mid-on, midwicket, square leg, deep square leg, deep point.
- Bouncer field : deep fine leg, deep square leg, short midwicket, with a leg slip if the batter is fending.
- Death field (T20) : long-off, long-on, deep point, deep third, deep square leg, deep midwicket, with only two or three fielders inside the circle besides the bowler and keeper.

Accuracy in fast bowling is measured by the proportion of deliveries landing in the intended zone. A commonly used coaching target is 70% of deliveries within a designated good-length corridor during a practice spell, with the remaining 30% distributed among planned variations.

Fast bowling is the most physically damaging cricket discipline. Bone-stress injuries of the lumbar spine are the characteristic fast-bowling injury, and are strongly associated with rapid increases in bowling volume rather than with high volume itself. Modern workload management therefore tracks the ratio of recent bowling load to longer-term average load, and limits overs per week for developing bowlers.

Scenario A - Test, first session, green surface, new ball. The plan is a good-to-full length on off stump with three slips and a gully. The bowler is attacking the outside edge and accepting that a driveable ball is part of the method. Success measure: plays-and-misses and edges, not necessarily economy.
Scenario B - ODI, overs 11-20, set batter, flat pitch. The plan is back of a length, wide-ish of off stump, with a deep point and deep midwicket. The objective is 3-4 dot balls per over, forcing the batter to take a risk. Change of pace is used on the fourth or fifth ball of the over.
Scenario C - T20, defending 11 from the final over. The bowler must deny the boundary rather than take wickets. First ball is the most important: a dot ball raises the required rate to above 11 per over. The plan is yorker, wide yorker, slower bouncer, yorker, wide yorker, yorker, with the field pushed back on the leg side.

Scenario D - Test, 45th over, dry surface, reverse swing available. The bowler comes round the wicket to a right-hander with a full length, targeting the base of the stumps. Two fielders are placed for the inside edge or leading edge - short midwicket and short cover - and the slip cordon is reduced to one.

The pace-versus-bat contest is best understood as a negotiation over length . The batter wants the bowler either full (driveable) or short (pullable); the bowler wants to sit on the good length that allows neither. Most tactical battles in a spell are attempts to move the other party off that length: a batter charging down the pitch tries to force the bowler shorter; a bouncer tries to force the batter back so that a full ball becomes lethal.
The corresponding batting perspective is set out in Document 01, section 6; the strategic framing of bowling changes and match-ups appears in Document 08.

Fast bowling combines a repeatable kinetic chain with a small set of high-skill variations. Pace itself is a threat, but the deliveries that take the most wickets are those that combine a good length with late movement - conventional swing with a new ball and reverse swing with an old one. Format determines the balance between wicket-taking and containment: Test bowling average, dot-ball percentage).

Spin bowling is the art of imparting rotation on the cricket ball so that it deviates off the pitch, and of using flight, pace and trajectory to deceive the batter in the air before it ever lands. Where fast bowling (Document 02) attacks primarily through speed and movement, spin bowling attacks primarily through deception . This is the spin-bowling member of a ten-document cricket corpus. It overlaps with Document 01 (batting against spin), Document 04 (wicketkeeping standing up to the stumps), Document 05 (close catchers and boundary riders), Document 06 (international formats and famous spinners), Document 07 (wides, stumpings and no-balls) and Document 08 (when to use spin). Typical speed range: 70-95 km/h for a wrist-spinner and 80-95 km/h for a finger-spinner, although modern limited-overs spinners frequently bowl above 95 km/h as a containment variation.

A spinning ball is acted on by four effects that the bowler can manipulate:
1. Turn - lateral deviation off the pitch, produced by the revolutions imparted at release and by the surface.
2. Drift - lateral movement in the air , produced by the Magnus effect on a ball spinning about a tilted axis. An off-spinner's drift moves the ball towards the leg side of a righthander before it turns back the other way.
3. Dip - downward curvature in flight caused by over-spin, which makes the ball fall shorter than the batter expects and is the reason a batter is caught out of position.
4. Bounce - the vertical deviation after pitching. Over-spin and a high release point both increase bounce.
The most dangerous spin delivery is not the one that turns the most, but the one that dips and then turns , because the batter has already misjudged the length before the deviation occurs.

Revolution rate determines how much work the ball can do; the axis of rotation determines the direction of that work. A pure side-spin axis produces maximum turn and minimum bounce; a pure over-spin axis produces maximum dip and bounce and minimum turn. Most effective spinners bowl with a tilted axis somewhere between the two.

The off-break is delivered by a right-arm bowler with the fingers rolling from the off side across the seam, so the ball turns from off to leg to a right-handed batter - that is, into the righthander and away from the left-hander. Grip : index and middle finger spread across the seam, with the index finger providing most of the spin; thumb light on the ball or off it entirely. Primary dismissals : bowled and LBW to the right-hander playing across the line; caught at slip or short leg off the outside edge or the bat-pad to a left-hander.

- Arm ball : bowled with a scrambled or upright seam and back-spin so that it holds its line and drifts with the arm instead of turning. Against a right-hander it threatens the outside edge; against a left-hander it threatens LBW.
- Doosra : turns the opposite way to the stock off-break, released from the back of the hand with the wrist turned. It is technically difficult and is subject to close scrutiny under the fifteen-degree elbow-extension tolerance permitted in the Laws.
- Carrom ball : flicked out from between the thumb and a bent middle finger. It can be made to turn either way depending on the release, and its principal value is that it is hard to detect from the hand.
- Undercutter : released with a flat, side-on axis so that the ball skids on low with minimal turn, used on slow or damp surfaces.
- Over-spinner : maximum top-spin for extra dip and bounce, aiming for a bat-pad catch.

Left-arm orthodox is finger spin bowled with the left hand. The ball turns from leg to off to a right-handed batter - away from the right-hander and into the left-hander. It is, in effect, the mirror image of off-spin. Tactical value : bowling over the wicket to a right-hander, the left-arm orthodox bowler pitches into the rough outside off stump created by the fast bowlers' follow-through, an area that becomes increasingly dangerous on days four and five of a Test match.

- Arm ball - holds its line and goes on with the angle.
- Undercutter - skids through low.
- Left-arm wrist spin (chinaman) - a distinct discipline rather than a variation: a left-handed wrist spinner whose stock ball turns into the right-hander, with a googly that turns away.

The leg-break is released with the wrist rotating from right to left (from the bowler's perspective), turning the ball from leg to off to a right-hander - away from the right-hander, into the left-hander. Grip : the ball rests across the first and second fingers with the third finger bent under the ball; the third finger provides the final flick. Why it is prized : the ball leaving the right-hander, with dip and bounce, produces both edges to slip and stumpings, and is the hardest delivery in cricket for a batter to control.

The googly is the wrist-spinner's central weapon precisely because it looks like the stock ball. Its value is lost if the batter can read it from the hand, which is why wrist-spinners work on disguising the wrist position at the top of the delivery arc.

Flight is the vertical trajectory of the delivery. A flighted ball is tossed above the batter's eye line, arriving on a steeper descending angle; a flat delivery is pushed through faster and lower. Flight is a risk-reward trade. A flighted ball invites the batter to advance down the pitch - creating the stumping chance and the catch to long-off - but a batter who reaches the pitch of the ball can hit it straight for six. A flat ball prevents the batter from using the feet but also makes it easier to work off the back foot for singles.

Speed variation is the most under-appreciated spin weapon. Changing pace by 8-10 km/h from one delivery to the next alters the length by roughly a metre from the batter's perspective without any change to the hand position, and is the mechanism behind many caught-andbowled and mistimed-drive dismissals.

Spinners vary the angle by using the full width of the crease - close to the stumps for LBW and bowled, wide of the crease to widen the turning angle, and round the wicket to attack the rough or to close the LBW angle to a left-hander.

This asymmetry is the reason a batting side may deliberately construct a left-hand/righthand combination in the middle order, since it forces the spinner to change line every time the strike is rotated, and forces the fielding captain to switch fielders between overs. The tactical use of this is treated in Document 08.

Rough patches are the scuffed areas created outside the line of the stumps by bowlers' followthrough. Because a bowler must not run onto the protected area of the pitch, the rough forms predominantly outside off stump to a left-hander (from a right-arm-over bowler) and outside leg stump to a right-hander from a left-arm-over bowler.

The spinner's role in a Test is to bowl long spells and to take wickets in the fourth innings. Key features:
- Willingness to concede runs in pursuit of wickets.
- Sustained accuracy over 20-30-over spells.
- Attacking fields: slip, short leg, silly point, catching midwicket.
- Use of the rough and the natural deterioration of the surface.

Spinners typically bowl in the middle overs (11-40), where four fielders are permitted outside the circle. The primary metrics become economy rate and middle-overs wickets . Wristspinners have become especially valuable in this phase because they can take wickets while other bowlers merely contain, breaking the partnership before the death overs.

In T20, spin is used in all three phases. The dominant methods are:
- Powerplay spin - bowling an off-spinner to a left-hander in the first two overs, using the turn away from the bat with only two fielders outside the circle.
- Middle-overs spin - flat, fast, and wide of off stump, with deep square and deep midwicket protecting the boundary.
- Death spin - wide yorker-length spin and back-of-a-length darts, relying on change of pace.
The T20 spinner's success metric is dot-ball percentage as much as wickets (Document 09).

Keeper up to the stumps, slip, leg slip, short leg, silly point, cover, mid-off, mid-on, midwicket, deep square leg (for the sweep). The two bat-pad fielders - short leg and silly point - exist because the off-break turning into the right-hander commonly produces a deflection off bat and pad.

Keeper up, point, cover, mid-off, mid-on, midwicket, deep midwicket, deep square leg, long-off, long-on. The sweeper on the leg side is the direct answer to the slog sweep; long-off and long-on cover the batter using the feet and hitting straight.

1. Set fields for the plan, not for the last shot played.
2. Protect the straight boundary against a batter who uses the feet; protect square when the batter sweeps.
3. A close catcher is only worth a place if the plan produces bat-pad chances.
4. Leave one deliberate gap and bowl to it - a spinner's field can invite a specific shot.
Field placement in general, including named positions, is set out in Document 05.

The set-up sequence. Spin dismissals are usually engineered over several deliveries. A common sequence for a leg-spinner to a right-hander: three leg-breaks on a fourth-stump line pushing the batter across, then a googly on the same line to strike the pad or take the inside edge. Attacking the sweeper. Against a batter who sweeps well, the spinner can bowl a fuller length on or outside off stump, making the sweep harder to control, or introduce a quicker, flatter ball to make the batter late on the shot. Bowling to a charging batter. Two responses: fire the ball flat and wide of off stump so the batter cannot reach it (the keeper standing up then has a stumping chance), or hold the ball back further and invite a catch to long-off. Bowling in partnership. Two spinners operating in tandem from both ends compress the
batter's options, because there is no over of relief in which to rotate strike easily.

Scenario A - Test, day four, dry and cracking, opposition chasing 280. The spinner attacks the rough outside off stump to the left-handers from over the wicket, with a slip, a silly point and a leg slip. The plan accepts singles into the leg side to keep the left-hander on strike. Scenario B - ODI, overs 20-30, two set batters, flat pitch. The wrist-spinner is brought on to break the partnership. The plan is a slightly flatter leg-break wide of off stump, with a deep point and a deep midwicket, and one flighted ball per over as the wicket-taking attempt. Scenario C - T20 powerplay, opposition opener is a left-hander. The off-spinner bowls over the wicket, turning the ball away from the left-hander, with only two fielders outside the circle. The plan depends on the batter having no natural boundary option through the off side. Scenario D - batter repeatedly using the feet. The spinner moves wide of the crease, bowls fractionally quicker and wider of off stump, and the keeper stands up to force the batter to
make ground back to the crease. Document 04 describes the keeping side of this dismissal.

Spin bowling wins its contests in the air as much as off the pitch. Drift and dip disturb the batter's judgement of length; turn and bounce exploit the resulting error. The finger spinner's asset is accuracy and repeatability, the wrist spinner's is the sheer difficulty of the ball leaving the bat. Format determines whether the spinner is asked to attack (Test cricket, fourth innings) or to contain (limited-overs middle overs), and the field setting must follow the plan rather than react to the previous delivery. The wicketkeeper is the only fielder permitted to wear gloves and external leg guards, and the only member of the fielding side who is involved in every single delivery of a match. This document is the wicketkeeping member of a ten-document cricket corpus. Primary scope : wicketkeeping technique, positioning, glove work, dismissals effected by the keeper, communication, and the keeper's tactical function. Declared overlaps : keeping to pace connects to Document 02 (fast bowling); keeping to spin and the stumping dismissal connect to Document 03 (spin bowling); the keeper's relationship with the slip cordon and the inner ring connects to Document 05 (fielding); the legal definition of stumping, run out, caught behind and the review process connects to Document 07 (Laws and playing conditions). Format-specific demands connect to Document 06 , and the keeper's input into captaincy connects to Document 08 .

1. Collect every delivery that the batter does not hit, preventing byes.
2. Catch edges - the keeper takes more catches than any other fielder in most teams.
3. Effect stumpings when the batter leaves the crease.
4. Receive throws from the field and complete run-outs at the striker's end.
5. Back up throws to the bowler's end when not directly involved.
6. Observe and inform - the keeper has the best view of swing, seam movement, spin, bounce and the batter's footwork, and is the captain's primary source of information.
7. Review advocacy - the keeper is usually the first person consulted before a DRS review.
8. Contribute with the bat - in modern international cricket the keeper is almost always a specialist batter as well.

The keeper watches the ball for its entire flight from a position directly behind the stumps. This produces information no other player has: the degree of late swing, whether the ball is holding its line off the pitch, how much the spinner is actually turning it, and whether the batter is planting the front foot or committing early. A keeper who does not communicate this is wasting the position.

- Feet : shoulder-width, weight on the balls of the feet, toes pointing slightly outwards.
- Knees : fully flexed so the hips sit low; the eye line should be at or just below the expected height of the ball as it passes the stumps.
- Hands : together, fingers pointing down, resting lightly on the ground or just above it, positioned between the feet.
- Head : still, eyes level.
- Rise : the keeper rises with the ball, not before it. Rising early is the single most common cause of dropped catches, because the hands come up through the line instead of tracking it.

Footwork is what allows the hands to be in the right place. Three movement patterns dominate:
1. Lateral shuffle - short, low sideways steps that keep the hips square to the line of the ball. The feet do not cross.
2. Cross-over step - for balls further from the body, the back foot crosses behind to cover more ground while the chest remains behind the hands.
3. Dive - used only when the ball cannot be reached with feet. The keeper pushes off the outside leg, keeps both hands together where possible, and presents both palms to the ball.
The governing principle: move to the line first, then to the height . A keeper who moves vertically before laterally ends up reaching across the body, which reduces the catching surface to one glove.

- Give with the ball. The hands travel backwards on impact, absorbing the pace. Rigid hands produce rebounds.
- Present the palms. Fingers point down for balls below the waist and up for balls above it. The transition between the two must be complete before the ball arrives; changing hand position midflight is a classic dropped-catch cause.
- Watch the ball into the gloves. The eyes must stay on the ball until it is in the hands, not on the batter or the stumps.
- Two hands where possible. One-handed takes are a last resort, not a style.

The leg-side take is the hardest routine skill in wicketkeeping because the batter's body blocks the sightline for part of the flight. Method: move early on the cue of the bowler's line, cross over behind the batter, and reacquire the ball as it passes the pads. Down-the-leg-side deliveries also generate the leg-side strangle - a faint edge that carries to the keeper - so the keeper must be moving and expecting a deflection simultaneously.
Standing back is used for fast and fast-medium bowling, where the ball would otherwise arrive too quickly and too high to be taken cleanly at the stumps.

Depth is set so that the ball reaches the keeper on the way down, at a comfortable height, having bounced once. Practical guides:
Express fast (145 km/h+), Approximate depth behind the stumps = 18-22 metres. Fast (135-145 km/h), Approximate depth behind the stumps = 15-18 metres. Fast-medium (125-135 km/h), Approximate depth behind the stumps = 12-15 metres. Medium (115-125 km/h), Approximate depth behind the stumps = 8-12 metres
Depth is adjusted for the surface: a low, slow pitch requires the keeper to come closer; a bouncy pitch requires standing deeper.

The keeper's depth sets the cordon's depth. Slips stand in line with, or fractionally behind, the keeper, and the first slip takes position roughly an arm's length plus a step from the keeper. If the keeper misjudges depth, the entire cordon is misplaced, and edges fall short. Document 05 treats the cordon in detail.

An edge off a fast bowler arrives with deviated pace and often with the same forward momentum. The keeper must not commit before the deflection: the correct method is to watch the ball onto the bat and react from there. Wide edges are taken diving, with both hands together if possible, because a two-handed diving take is more reliable than a one-handed one at equivalent reach.

Standing up compresses reaction time to roughly 0.2-0.3 seconds from the ball pitching. The consequences:
- The keeper cannot rely on anticipation of line; the hands must react.
- The head must stay outside the line of the stumps to keep the sightline clear.
- The gloves must be behind the stumps at the moment of collection, not in front, or the keeper risks taking the ball in front of the wicket - which for a stumping would be illegal and for a catch invites injury.
- The keeper must not move in front of the stumps before the ball passes the bat, as this can constitute an unfair obstruction of the striker.

Keeping to the off-spinner (Document 03) means expecting the ball to turn into a right-handed batter - that is, towards the keeper's leg side. Keeping to the leg-spinner means expecting it to turn away , towards the off side and the slip cordon, with the googly reversing that expectation without warning. Practical rules:

The doosra and the carrom ball present the greatest difficulty, because if the keeper cannot read them from the hand, the keeper must react purely from the pitch - which is the same problem the batter has, with less time.

The most common keeper dismissal. Requirements: the ball must touch the bat or the glove holding the bat, and must be caught cleanly before touching the ground. The keeper is frequently the appealing party because the sound and deviation are clearest from behind.

The striker is out stumped if, while not attempting a run, the striker is out of the crease and the wicket is put down by the keeper with the ball, without the intervention of another fielder. Essential technical points:
- The keeper must take the ball behind the stumps , not in front of them.
- The hands should travel towards the stumps with the ball already gripped - the take and the break should be a single motion.
- Speed matters more than force: the bails need only be dislodged.
- Against a batter who overbalances, the keeper should aim to break the wicket nearest to the batter's grounded foot.
The full legal definition, including the interaction with no-balls and stumpings off wides, appears in Document 07.

At the striker's end, the keeper receives throws from the field. Technique:
- Position beside the stumps, not directly behind, so the gloves and the stumps are both in view of the throw.
- Take the ball in front of the body and then bring it to the stumps; do not attempt to catch the ball on the stumps unless the run-out is extremely tight.
- Call the throwing fielder to the appropriate end loudly and early.

A keeper's appeal carries weight because the keeper hears the contact. A keeper who appeals indiscriminately loses that credibility with the umpire, the captain and the review process - which is a genuine tactical cost, not merely an etiquette point.

The keeper is effectively a second captain, standing in the best observation position. Typical keeper-driven suggestions: bringing in a bat-pad fielder when a spinner starts to grip, moving a slip to gully when edges are travelling square, or recommending a bowling change when the ball stops swinging.

The keeper directs traffic: calling which end a throw should go to, calling catches in the keeper-slip overlap region ('keeper's' or 'yours'), and setting the cordon's depth. The convention is that the keeper's call takes precedence over the slip's in the overlap zone, because the keeper is moving towards the ball with momentum.

Concentration. A Test keeper may face 500+ deliveries in a day, most requiring no action. The discipline is a switch-on/switch-off cycle: full focus from the bowler's load-up to the completion of the delivery, deliberate relaxation between balls. Keepers who maintain constant intensity fatigue and drop catches in the final session.

Floodlit conditions change ball visibility, particularly with a white ball against a dark sightscreen background, and with a pink ball in day-night Test cricket, where the twilight period is the most difficult phase. Dew is the dominant variable: a wet ball is heavier, skids on faster, and is significantly harder to grip for both take and stumping. Keepers commonly stand fractionally deeper in heavy dew.

The keeper's contribution to the review decision is a recognised tactical skill, because reviews are a limited resource (see Document 07 for the mechanics, Document 08 for review strategy). The keeper contributes:
- For caught behind : whether a sound was heard, whether deviation was seen, and whether the sound coincided with the ball passing the bat rather than the pad.
- For LBW : whether the ball pitched in line, whether there was an inside edge, and the height at impact - though the keeper's height judgement is less reliable than the bowler's or the slip's because of the flat viewing angle.
- For stumping : in most playing conditions the stumping is automatically referred to the third umpire when the keeper appeals, so no team review is consumed.
A well-drilled side has an explicit rule for who decides: usually the bowler and the keeper together, within the fifteen-second window, with the captain arbitrating.

- Lower-body endurance : the keeper performs several hundred deep squats per day in a Test match. Posterior-chain and quadriceps endurance is the limiting physical factor.
- Reaction time : standing up to spin leaves 0.2-0.3 seconds; this is trained with short-range reaction drills using deflected or randomised deliveries rather than predictable feeds.
- Hand conditioning : repeated impact from fast bowling requires progressive glove-hand conditioning; finger injuries are the characteristic keeping injury.
- Concentration training : structured switch-on/switch-off routines, often anchored to a physical cue such as tapping the gloves as the bowler begins the run-up.

Wicketkeeping has evolved from a purely specialist defensive role into a dual batting-and-keeping role. Adam Gilchrist of Australia is widely regarded as the player who accelerated that change, combining high-quality glovework with aggressive top-order-standard batting from the middle order. Mark Boucher of South Africa and Kumar Sangakkara of Sri Lanka are frequently cited for volume of dismissals and longevity, Sangakkara also being a leading batter who kept for part of his career. MS Dhoni of India is particularly associated with rapid stumpings and with the keeper-as-captain model, having led India while keeping. Historically, keepers such as Alan Knott and Bob Taylor of England and Syed Kirmani of India were noted primarily for the purity of their glovework, especially standing up to spin.
Document 10 discusses specific historic performances in their full match context.

- Standing up - keeping immediately behind the stumps.
- Standing back - keeping at a distance appropriate to pace bowling.
- Take - the act of collecting the ball cleanly.
- Soft hands / giving with the ball - absorbing pace by withdrawing the hands on impact.
- Leg-side strangle - a dismissal caught behind off a ball drifting down the leg side.
- Bat-pad - a deflection off bat then pad (or pad then bat) taken by a close catcher.
- Byes - runs scored when the ball passes the batter and the keeper without touching bat or body.
- Stumping - dismissal by breaking the wicket while the striker is out of the crease and not attempting a run.
- Cordon - the keeper plus the slip fielders, treated as one catching unit.

Wicketkeeping is defined by repetition and by consequence: hundreds of routine collections punctuated by a handful of chances that decide matches. The technical core is small - stay down, move to the line, give with the ball, take behind the stumps - but it must survive fatigue, poor light, dew, variable bounce and the unpredictability of spin. The modern keeper is additionally a tactical hub, feeding information to the captain, advising on reviews, and contributing substantial runs.

Fielding is the collective activity of the nine players who are neither bowling nor keeping wicket, together with the bowler and keeper once the ball is in play. It is the only cricket discipline in which every member of the side participates continuously. Primary scope : fielding technique (catching, ground fielding, throwing), the named fielding positions, and the tactical logic of field setting. Declared overlaps : catching positions behind the wicket connect to Document 04 (wicketkeeping); fields for pace and spin connect to Documents 02 and 03 ; the shots that fields are designed to stop connect to Document 01 ; fielding restrictions and the thirty-yard circle connect to Document 07 ; the captaincy reasoning behind field changes connects to Document 08 .

1. Catching - converting chances into dismissals.
2. Ground fielding - stopping and retrieving the ball to deny runs.
3. Throwing - returning the ball accurately and quickly to create run-outs.
A commonly used coaching framing is that fielding saves or costs a team a measurable number of runs per match, and that in closely contested limited-overs matches the fielding differential is often larger than the bowling differential.

Before each delivery every fielder adopts a ready position: feet shoulder-width, knees flexed, weight forward on the balls of the feet, hands in front of the body, eyes on the bat. The fielder should be walking in as the bowler runs in, so that momentum is already forward at the moment of contact. A stationary fielder is slower to react in every direction.

Used in the outfield and at mid-off/mid-on for lofted shots.
- Get under the ball early and set the feet; do not drift into position at the last moment.
- Use the reverse cup (fingers up, thumbs together) for balls above the head, and the orthodox cup (fingers down, little fingers together) for balls below the chest.
- Watch the ball into the hands and give slightly on impact.
- In sunlight, use the non-catching hand as a shade, or move sideways to remove the sun from the line.
- On the boundary, establish the boundary line position first, then track the ball.

- Get the hands beneath the expected height of the ball, fingers pointing down.
- Attack the ball - moving forward converts a bouncing ball into a catch.
- Keep the head low and the eyes level with the ball where possible.

Slip catching is a distinct skill with its own technique:
- Stance : a low, wide crouch with the hands resting between the feet, weight forward.
- Sightline : watch the edge of the bat, not the ball in flight. Watching the ball from the bowler's hand causes the eyes to track past the bat and lose the deflection.
- Hands : react from the hands, not from a step. A slip fielder who steps before the hands move arrives late.
- Give : take the ball with soft hands; slip catches arrive with full pace.

Modern boundary catching includes the relay catch, in which a fielder catches the ball while momentum carries them over the rope, releases it before grounding outside the boundary, and either re-enters to complete the catch or passes it to a supporting fielder. The Laws governing the moment of contact with the boundary and the fielder's grounding are summarised in Document 07.

Used when a run-out is possible. The fielder attacks the ball, picks up one-handed with the throwing hand beside the leading foot, and releases in the same motion. The head must stay down through the pick-up; lifting the head to look at the stumps before the ball is secured is the standard cause of fumbles.

Used when the priority is certainty, not speed. The fielder turns side-on, drops the trailing knee to the ground beside the heel of the leading foot, forming a barrier with no gap, and takes the ball with both hands in front of the body. Appropriate for hard-hit balls on uneven outfields and for boundary-saving work.

On fast outfields, a fielder chasing a ball towards the rope slides feet-first or hip-first, stopping the ball with one or both hands and flicking it back infield before contact with the boundary. Whether the boundary is scored depends on the fielder's contact with the rope while in possession of the ball.

- Grip : across the seam, using three fingers for maximum control.
- Alignment : the non-throwing shoulder points at the target; the front arm pulls down through the throw.
- Release : over the top, with the aim at the top of the stumps, so that a bouncing throw still arrives at collectable height.
- Follow-through : the throwing arm continues across the body; the back leg comes through.

A direct hit - throwing down the stumps without a fielder collecting - is the highest-value fielding act because it removes the reaction time of the receiving player. Coaching emphasis: aim at the base of the stumps for underarm attempts from close range, and at the top for longer throws. The practical hit rate is low, which is why the decision to attempt a direct hit rather than throw to the keeper is a risk judgement: a missed direct hit with no backing-up fielder concedes overthrows.

For every throw there must be a fielder behind the receiving stumps. Failure to back up converts a missed throw into extra runs. The convention: the bowler backs up the keeper's end; a mid-off or mid-on fielder backs up the bowler's end.

The square-leg umpire normally stands at square leg, and a fielder may not be placed where the umpire's view is obstructed; the umpire will move to the off side if a fielding side wants a fielder in that exact position.

1. Set fields for the plan, not the last ball. Reactive field changes tell the batter what worked.
2. Balance the sides. No more than two fielders may be behind square on the leg side (Document 07); exceeding this is a no-ball.
3. Leave a deliberate gap. A field can invite a specific shot. Leaving cover open and bowling a length that makes the cover drive risky is a trap, not an oversight.
4. Protect the batter's strength only when the cost is acceptable. In Test cricket, a captain may deliberately allow a batter's favourite shot in order to keep a catcher in place.
5. Match the field to the ball's age. A new ball justifies slips; a 40-over-old ball in an ODI justifies boundary riders.

When a left-hander and a right-hander bat together, every single rotates the strike and mirrors the field. The fielding side must either reset several fielders between deliveries - which slows the over rate - or set a compromise field that suits neither plan fully. This is one of the strongest reasons batting sides construct mixed-handed partnerships. The tactical treatment appears in Document 08.
A run-out requires three components: the stop, the throw and the take. The failure point is usually the transition between them.

1. Is a run-out realistically available? If not, prioritise a clean stop and a return to the keeper.
2. If yes, which end? The end where the batter has furthest to travel, which is usually the end the batters are turning back for.
3. Direct hit or throw to a player? Direct hit only if the fielder is close and balanced; otherwise throw to the gloves.
4. Is there a backing-up fielder? If not, the risk of overthrows raises the threshold for attempting the direct hit.

The captain owns the field, but the working practice in most international sides is collaborative: the bowler proposes a plan, the captain sets the field consistent with it, and the keeper offers observational input. Once the bowler begins the run-up, no further field changes are possible without the delivery being called dead.
Communication protocol : fielders call for catches by name or position; the keeper's call takes precedence in the keeper-slip overlap; the fielder moving forward has priority over the fielder moving backwards on a shared chance, because the forward-moving fielder has the better sightline and is more likely to complete the catch.
Over rate. Frequent field changes cost time. Because over-rate penalties apply in international cricket, a captain must balance tactical precision against the clock (Document 07).

Fielding converts bowling plans into dismissals and converts athleticism into saved runs. The technical content is comparatively simple - catch with soft hands, attack the ball, throw over the top, back up every throw - but the tactical content is deep, because every field is a statement about which shots the bowling side is willing to concede. A well-set field constrains the batter's options before the ball is bowled; a reactive field merely reports what has already gone wrong. International cricket is cricket played between national representative teams under the sanction of the International Cricket Council (ICC). It is organised around three recognised formats - Test cricket, One Day Internationals and Twenty20 Internationals - each with its own structure, rhythm and tactical character. Primary scope : the structure, history and competitive architecture of international cricket, and the way format determines the nature of the contest. Declared overlaps : the precise regulations governing each format are set out in Document 07 ; formatdriven tactics appear in Document 08 ; format-specific statistical norms appear in Document 09 ; individual historic matches are treated in depth in Document 10 . Skill-level treatments of batting, bowling, keeping and fielding by format appear in Documents 01-05 .

Cricket developed in England and spread through British colonial and commercial networks during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The first match now recognised as a Test was played between Australia and England at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in March 1877; Australia won by 45 runs. The Ashes originated from Australia's victory at The Oval in 1882, after which a mock obituary published in an English newspaper declared that English cricket had died and that 'the body will be cremated and the ashes taken to Australia'. The resulting England-Australia Test series has been contested under that name ever since, and remains the sport's oldest continuous rivalry.

Test status was granted gradually. South Africa joined the Test-playing group in the 1880s, followed by the West Indies, New Zealand and India in the 1920s and 1930s, Pakistan in the early 1950s, Sri Lanka in the early 1980s, Zimbabwe in 1992, Bangladesh in 2000, and Afghanistan and Ireland in 2017. South Africa did not play international cricket between 1970 and 1991 owing to the international sporting boycott associated with apartheid, returning to international competition in 1991-92.

The first One Day International was played between Australia and England at Melbourne in January 1971, arranged after the abandonment of a rain-affected Test. It was played over 40 eight-ball overs per side. The format's commercial viability was established rapidly, and the first Cricket World Cup followed in England in 1975, contested over 60 overs per side.
Twenty20 was introduced as a domestic English competition in 2003 and reached international level shortly afterwards, with the first ICC World Twenty20 staged in South Africa in 2007.

The ICC is the global governing body. Its principal functions include sanctioning international matches, appointing the elite panel of umpires and match referees, administering the playing conditions that supplement the Laws, operating anti-corruption and anti-doping programmes, maintaining team and player rankings, and organising global events.
Members are classified as Full Members - the nations with permanent Test status - and Associate Members . Associate nations can hold ODI and T20I status without holding Test status; since 2018, all ICC members have T20I status for men's and women's international matches between members, which substantially expanded the number of recognised T20I nations.

The Laws of Cricket are owned and maintained by Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC), not by the ICC. The ICC issues playing conditions that modify or supplement the Laws for international matches - for example, the number of overs, fielding restrictions, the Decision Review System, free hits and over-rate penalties. This distinction is important and is treated in detail in Document 07.

The draw is the defining feature of Test cricket: a match in which neither side is dismissed twice or overtakes the required total within the available time. A draw is distinct from a tie , which occurs only when the scores are level and the side batting last has been dismissed. Ties in Test cricket are exceptionally rare - only two have occurred, in 1960 (Australia v West Indies, Brisbane) and 1986 (India v Australia, Madras, now Chennai).

- The follow-on : if the side batting second trails by a defined margin (200 runs in a five-day match), the side batting first may require them to bat again immediately.
- The declaration : a captain may close an innings voluntarily at any point.
- Deterioration : the pitch changes across five days, usually favouring spin later, which makes the toss and the batting order more consequential than in limited-overs cricket.
- Sessions : strategy is organised session by session rather than over by over.

The ICC World Test Championship, introduced with its first cycle running from 2019 to 2021, provides league context for bilateral Test series. Teams accumulate points from series played within a two-year cycle, standings are expressed as a percentage of available points (to accommodate unequal numbers of matches), and the top two sides contest a final. This was the first sustained attempt to give Test cricket a global competitive structure rather than leaving it purely bilateral.

Day-night Test cricket was introduced in November 2015, with Australia and New Zealand playing the first pink-ball Test at Adelaide Oval. The pink ball is used because the traditional red ball becomes difficult to see under floodlights, while the white ball used in limited-overs cricket deteriorates too quickly for Test-length innings. Characteristic effects reported from pink-ball cricket include a distinct twilight period in which batting is notably harder, and increased lateral movement under lights.

Totals that were once exceptional became routine: 300 moved from a match-winning score to a par score at many venues, and 400 has been exceeded on multiple occasions.

T20 compresses every decision. A bowler's four overs cannot be recovered; a batter's dismissal costs a disproportionate share of the innings; a single over can decide the match. The format has driven specific skill development: the ramp and scoop for batters, the wide yorker and knuckle ball for bowlers, and the matchup as an organising tactical principle (Document 08).

Domestic franchise T20 leagues - most prominently the Indian Premier League, launched in 2008, along with competitions in Australia, the Caribbean, England, Pakistan, Bangladesh, South Africa and elsewhere - have significantly affected international cricket. Effects include the professionalisation of players from smaller cricketing nations, the rapid global transfer of technical innovations, and increasing pressure on the international scheduling calendar.

The ICC maintains separate team rankings for Tests, ODIs and T20Is, and separate player rankings for batting, bowling and all-round performance. Team rankings are calculated from results over a rolling recent period, weighted by the strength of the opposition, so a win against a higher-ranked side contributes more than a win against a lower-ranked one. Player rankings are a points-based rating rather than a simple average, and are adjusted for match context including the quality of opposition and pitch conditions.

DRS allows a team to challenge an on-field decision within a defined period after the ball becomes dead. The system combines ball-tracking, edge-detection and replay. Two concepts are central:
- Umpire's call - where ball-tracking shows a marginal outcome for an LBW review, the on-field decision stands. This preserves the primacy of the on-field umpire in marginal cases.
- Review retention - an unsuccessful review lost only to umpire's call does not cost the reviewing team a review under current conditions.

International cricket is not one sport played at three lengths, but three distinct competitive problems sharing a common skill base. Test cricket rewards endurance, technical soundness and the capacity to build advantage over days. ODI cricket rewards phase management and the controlled conversion of wickets in hand into late acceleration. T20 rewards precision under compression, where a single over can be decisive. The governance layer - the ICC's playing conditions, ranking systems and event calendar - shapes how these formats interact, while home conditions remain the single largest external variable in bilateral cricket.

Cricket is governed by the Laws of Cricket , a codified body of rules owned and maintained by Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC). Competitions layer playing conditions on top of the Laws to define format-specific matters such as the number of overs, fielding restrictions and review systems. Primary scope : the Laws, the officials who apply them, the dismissal types, the extras, and the distinction between Law and playing condition. Declared overlaps : the stumping and caught-behind dismissals connect to Document 04 ; fielding restrictions and boundary law connect to Document 05 ; format structures connect to Document 06 ; the tactical exploitation of reviews, free hits and declarations connects to Document 08 ; no-ball and wide definitions connect to Documents 02 and 03 . A critical distinction used throughout this document : a Law applies to all cricket unless varied; a playing condition applies only to a specific competition. Powerplays, DRS, free hits and over-rate penalties are playing conditions, not Laws. Where this document states a number for a playing condition, that number reflects standard international playing conditions, which are revised periodically.

The Laws are organised into numbered Laws covering, in sequence: the players and officials; the equipment and the field of play; the structure of the match (innings, overs, intervals); scoring and results; the ball in play (dead ball, no-ball, wide, byes and leg byes); the ten methods of dismissal; the fielder's conduct; and fair and unfair play, including the Spirit of Cricket preamble. Two structural features are worth noting:
1. Dismissal methods are exhaustively enumerated. There are exactly ten, and no other means of dismissal exists.
2. The umpires are the sole judges of fair and unfair play , with authority beyond the literal text where conduct is concerned.

A striker is out LBW if all the following are satisfied:
1. The delivery is not a no-ball.
2. The ball does not pitch outside leg stump.
3. The ball strikes the striker (other than the bat or the hand holding the bat) in line with the stumps, or outside the line of off stump when the striker is not attempting a genuine shot.
4. The ball would have gone on to hit the stumps.
5. The ball did not first touch the bat or the glove holding the bat.
The interaction of conditions 2 and 3 is the source of most misunderstanding: a ball pitching outside off stump and striking the pad in line is out; a ball pitching outside leg stump can never be out, however plumb it appears; a ball striking the pad outside the line of off stump is out only if no shot was offered.

If the striker leaves the crease after a delivery and the keeper breaks the wicket, the dismissal is a stumping if the striker was not attempting a run, and a run out if a run was being attempted. The distinction matters because a stumping is credited to the bowler and a run out is not (Document 09).

The incoming batter must be ready to face, or the non-striker must be ready, within the time specified by the playing conditions (three minutes in the Laws; two minutes under many international playing conditions). This dismissal is extremely rare in international cricket.

An umpire may not give a batter out unless the fielding side appeals, conventionally with the phrase 'How's that?'. Key procedural points:
- An appeal covers all modes of dismissal; the umpire adjudicates whichever applies.
- The fielding side may withdraw an appeal with the umpire's consent, and the batter is then reinstated.
- If the bowler's-end umpire is unsighted, the appeal may be referred to the striker's-end umpire.
- Not out decisions may also be reviewed, so a decision is not final until the review window closes.

For LBW reviews, ball-tracking outputs three assessments: pitching , impact and wickets hitting . If any of these is marginal - within a defined tolerance - the result is umpire's call , and the on-field decision stands, whether it was out or not out. Under current playing conditions the reviewing team does not lose a review when the only reason for the decision standing is umpire's call.
This is the most commonly misunderstood element of the Laws-and-conditions framework, because the same ball-tracking output can produce 'out' for one review and 'not out' for another, depending on what the onfield umpire originally decided.

Separately from player reviews, the on-field umpires may refer certain decisions themselves - most commonly catches where the ball may have carried, run-outs, stumpings and boundary judgements. These do not consume a team's reviews.

DLS adjusts targets in rain-interrupted limited-overs matches. Its conceptual basis is that a batting side's scoring potential depends on two resources: overs remaining and wickets in hand . A published resource table gives the percentage of total resources available for any combination of the two. The revised target is calculated from the ratio of the two sides' available resources. A minimum number of overs must be bowled to each side for a result to be possible - typically 20 overs per side in ODIs and 5 in T20Is.

International playing conditions specify a minimum over rate. Penalties have included fines, WTC points deductions in Test cricket, and in-match penalties in limited-overs cricket requiring an additional fielder inside the circle for the remaining overs if the side falls behind the required rate.

- Law - a rule of cricket maintained by MCC, applying universally unless varied.
- Playing condition - a competition-specific regulation supplementing or modifying the Laws.
- Popping crease - the line four feet in front of the stumps that defines the batter's ground and the bowler's front-foot limit.
- Return crease - the side lines defining the bowler's back-foot limit.
- Dead ball - the state in which the ball is out of play.
- Free hit - a delivery, following a no-ball under limited-overs conditions, from which the striker cannot be bowled, caught or given LBW.
- Umpire's call - the DRS outcome where a marginal result leaves the on-field decision standing.
- Follow-on - the requirement for a trailing side to bat again immediately.
- Short run - a run not counted because the batter failed to ground behind the crease.

The Laws define what is possible in cricket; playing conditions define what is possible in a particular competition. Most public confusion about cricket's rules arises from conflating the two, or from the interaction between simple-sounding conditions - as with LBW, where five separate requirements must all be satisfied. The officiating structure has evolved from two on-field umpires with unaided judgement to a layered system in which the on-field umpire's decision remains the default and technology intervenes only where the evidence is conclusive.

Selection is a strategic commitment made before information is available. The recurring trade-offs:
- Batting depth vs bowling options. Playing an extra batter protects against collapse but leaves the captain with fewer bowling choices if a bowler is ineffective.
- Specialist vs all-rounder. An all-rounder provides flexibility at some cost in peak quality in both disciplines.
- Spin/pace balance. Determined by the pitch, the opposition's handedness distribution, and the length of the match.
- Match-up selection. Choosing a left-arm spinner because the opposition's top order contains four right-handers is a selection-level match-up decision.

Dot-ball pressure is cumulative. A sequence of dot balls raises the required rate and induces a higher-risk shot, which produces the wicket. The batting counter is strike rotation: converting a would-be dot into a single transfers the problem to a different bowler-batter pairing and resets the field. Boundary targeting is the deliberate selection of which bowler and which phase to attack. A common
limited-overs approach is to identify the fifth bowling option - often a part-timer or the weakest of five - and plan to take 30+ runs from their overs while treating the specialists with respect.

- The first twenty balls together are the highest-risk phase of any partnership; the convention is to survive them before setting a target rate.
- Role allocation : one anchor and one aggressor, with the roles reversible if the aggressor is dismissed.
- Farming the strike : a set batter deliberately takes the majority of deliveries when partnered with a tail-ender, typically by taking a single from the fifth or sixth ball of the over.

The reasons a captain changes the bowling:
1. A bowler has lost effectiveness - rising economy, loss of movement, visible fatigue.
2. A match-up is available - bringing on the bowler whose stock delivery leaves the incoming batter.
3. A new batter has arrived - the best wicket-taking bowler should face a new batter in their first ten deliveries.
4. Conditions have changed - the ball has begun reversing, or the lights have come on.
5. Resource management - a T20 bowler's four overs must be distributed across phases.

Bowling in partnership means pairing bowlers whose plans complement each other: one bowler applying containment pressure while the other attacks, or two bowlers who move the ball in opposite directions so the batter cannot settle on one line. Two spinners in tandem from both ends is the classic Test example (Document 03).
